en: The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Simile of the Rice Seedling Explaining Dependent Origination, Spoken by the Bodhisattva Maitreya;
[Translated during the reign of] Kai-fu Yi-tong San-si Te-jin Shi Hong-lu Qing.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Da Guangzhi Daxingshan Monastery, who was the Duke of Sù with a fief of three thousand households, invested with purple robes, posthumously honored as Minister of Works, and bestowed the title Dàjiàn (Great Mirror). By Imperial Decree: Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Bhagavat was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, as well as a multitude of great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra went to the place where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya was walking.
There, the Bodhisattva Maitreya and Śāriputra sat together upon a flat rock.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra asked the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya:
"Today the World-Honored One, observing the rice seedlings, addressed the bhikṣus and spoke these words: 'O bhikṣus!'"
"If one sees dependent origination, one sees the Dharma;
if one sees the Dharma, one sees the Buddha.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One remained silent.
What is the meaning of this sutra spoken by the Tathāgata?
What is dependent origination?
And what is the Dharma?
What is this Buddha?
How is it that by seeing dependent origination one sees the Dharma,
and how is it that by seeing the Dharma one sees the Buddha?
Having spoken these words, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"The Bhagavat has frequently taught this meaning to the bhikṣus:
'If one sees dependent origination, one sees the Dharma;'"

"If one sees the Dharma, one sees the Buddha. Regarding dependent origination: it is said that ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions existence; existence conditions birth; and birth conditions aging and death.
The Tathāgata has taught that this is dependent origination. What is the Dharma?
The Tathāgata has briefly explained that the attainment of nirvāṇa through the eightfold noble path is called the Dharma.

What is a Buddha? Because he has awakened to all phenomena, having realized nirvana with the eye of noble wisdom and perceived the dharmas to be practiced for the sake of awakening—he is called a Buddha.
"How does one see dependent origination?

The Tathāgata has taught that this dependent origination is eternally abiding; it is without a person, without a self, without a sentient being, without a life-span; it is non-perverted, unarisen, uncreated, unconditioned, without opposition, and without obstruction."
To see that the intrinsic nature is quiescent is to see the Dharma.

To see it as being of such a kind—permanent, devoid of a person, devoid of a self, devoid of a sentient being, devoid of a life-span, non-perverted, unarisen, without opposition, and without obstruction—is to see the Dharma.
"From this point onward, one immediately beholds the Dharma-body, attains the vision of the Tathāgata, and realizes perfect wisdom through direct experience.
He asked again:
"What is the meaning of 'dependent origination'?"

He replied: "There is a cause and there is a condition; it is not without cause or condition that it is called 'dependent origination. Within this context, the Tathāgata has briefly explained the characteristics of dependent origination."
For this reason, these fruits are able to arise.

Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthititā), the fixed course of phenomena (dharma-niyāmatā), conformity with dependent origination, suchness (tathatā), non-erroneous suchness, unalterable suchness, true non-alterability, reality, non-perversion, and non-delusion remain as they are.
"Furthermore, that which arises through dependent origination originates from two kinds of causes.
What are these two? First, dependence upon causes; second, dependence upon conditions."
One should understand that these dependently arisen phenomena are of two kinds: namely, the external and the internal.
Regarding the external dependent origination, what is its causal connection?

It is as follows: from a seed arises a sprout; from a sprout arises a leaf; from a leaf arises a branch; from a branch arises a stalk; from a stalk arises a trunk; from a trunk arises a flower; and from a flower arises a fruit.
If there were no seed, the sprout would have nothing from which to arise; even up to the flowers and fruits, they too would have nothing from which to arise.
Because the seed exists, the sprout arises; even up to the flower producing the fruit, the seed does not form this thought:
"I am able to produce the sprout."
The sprout also does not form this thought:
"I am produced from the seed.
This continues up to the flower, which likewise does not form such a thought.
"The flower thinks, 'I can produce the fruit,' but the fruit also does not have this thought:
'I am produced from the flower.'"
"Nevertheless, because there is a seed, a sprout arises, and so on until, because there is a flower, fruit is produced.
In this way, one should understand that external dependent origination is bound to causes.
How is external dependent origination bound to conditions?"
What is called "dependent origination through the conjunction of the six elements" is dependent upon conditions.
What are the six elements?
They are earth, water, fire, wind, space, and time; their conjunction constitutes dependent origination dependent upon conditions.
What are the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and time?
That which causes the seed to be maintained is called the earth element;
that which causes the seed to be moistened is called the water element.
That which causes the seed to achieve its potential is called the fire element;
that which causes the seed to grow is called the wind element;
that which causes the seed to be without obstruction is called the space element.
That which causes the seed to undergo transformation is called the element of time (*kāyadhātu*).
If the various conditions are absent, the seed will not produce a sprout.
However, if there is no deficiency in the element of earth, and no deficiency in the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and time, then all being combined, the seed produces a sprout.
The earth element does not form this thought:
"I am able to sustain the seeds.
The water element does not form this thought:
"The water element thinks: 'I can moisten the seed.
The fire element does not think:
'I can bring the seed to maturity.'"
The wind element does not form this thought:
"I am able to cause the seed to grow.
The space element does not form this thought:
"I can cause the seed to be free from obstacles.
At that time, the element does not form this thought:
"I can transform the seed."
Furthermore, the seed does not form this thought:
"I have produced the sprout by means of various conditions.

Nevertheless, when a seed produces a sprout through such conditions, that sprout is not self-made, not made by another, not made by both together, not made by the Lord (Īśvara), not produced by the transformation of time, not born of its own inherent nature, and does not arise without depending on a creator; rather, it arises from causes.
In this way, the seed arises through the conjunction of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and time.
Furthermore, one should know that these factors of dependent origination possess five characteristics:

they are neither eternal nor annihilated; there is no transmigration; from a small cause a great fruit arises; and there is a continuous succession of similar states without the production of dissimilar things.
Why is it not eternal?
Because the seed and the sprout are distinct, the seed itself is not the sprout, yet the sprout does not arise through the destruction of the seed.
Rather, the sprout arises precisely because the seed has perished; since the sprout is born from the perishing of the seed, it is called "not eternal."
What is meant by "not severed"?
First, the sprout arises from a seed that has not been destroyed, yet it is also not the case that it is not destroyed.
In this way, when the seed is destroyed and the conditions harmonize to produce the shoot, it is called "not severed."
Regarding "non-transference": this is because the seed and the sprout are distinct.
Regarding "the cause being small while the fruit is great": the seed is small, yet the fruit is abundant.
Regarding "similar continuity": according to the seed that is planted, the harvest of fruit is likewise so.
Thus, one should know that external dependent origination has five aspects.
What is internal dependent origination?
It arises in two ways.
What are the two kinds? First, that which is bound to causes; second, that which is bound to conditions.
How is it that internal dependently arisen phenomena are bound to causes?
That which is called "ignorance conditions volitional formations," and so on, up to "birth conditions aging and death.

If there were no ignorance, then there would be no volitional formations; however, because ignorance exists, there are volitional formations, and so on, until birth conditions aging and death, whereby they come to arise.
That ignorance does not form this thought:
"I am able to produce volitional formations.
Volitional formations do not form this thought:
"I am born from ignorance," and so on,
up to birth not forming the thought:
"I can produce old age and death."
"However, where there is ignorance, there is the arising of volitional formations; and so on, until: where there is birth, there is the arising of old age and death.
In this way, the internal dependently arisen phenomena are bound to causes."
"How are the internally dependently arisen phenomena connected to their conditions?
They arise from the conjunction of the six elements.
What is the conjunction of the six elements?"
That which is called the conjunction of the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness, arising through conditions and bound to those conditions.
What is the earth element?
That which causes the body to aggregate as a solid substance is called the earth element.
What is the water element?
That which causes the body to maintain cohesion is called the water element.
What is the fire element?
That which causes the food and drink within the body to be digested is called the fire element (*tejodhātu*).
What is the wind element (*vāyudhātu*)?
That which causes inhalation and exhalation to occur within the body is called the wind element.
What is the space element?
That which forms cavities and apertures within the body is called the space element.
What is the consciousness element?

It causes name-and-form (nāmarūpa) to revolve like a bundle of reeds; the out-flowing mental consciousness associated with the five sensory consciousnesses is called the element of consciousness (vijñānadhātu).
Without these six elements, the body would not be formed.
If the internal earth element is not deficient, and the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are also not deficient, then through their complete integration, the body is produced.
The earth element does not think:
"I am able to aggregate the body and form its solid substance.
The water element does not think:
"I am able to provide cohesion for the body.
The fire element does not think:
"I am able to bring about the digestion of food and drink within the body."
The wind element does not think:
"I am able to cause the body to produce inhalation and exhalation.
The space element does not think:
"I can create cavities within the body.
Nor does the consciousness element (vijñānadhātu) form this thought:
"I can transform name-and-form (nāmarūpa), just like bundles of reeds."
That body, moreover, does not form this thought:
"I am produced by these various conditions.
Nevertheless, it is through such various conditions that the body arises.

This earth element is without self, without person, without life, without a life-sustainer, without a being born of mind, without a youth, without female, without male, without that which is neither male nor female, without "I," and likewise without anything else.

The elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are likewise without a self, without a person, without a life-force, without a soul, without a being born of mind, without a youth, without female, without male, without that which is neither male nor female, without a "mine," and without anything else.

"What is ignorance? It is the arising, with respect to these six elements, of a single notion, a notion of unity, a notion of permanence, a notion of solidity, a notion of eternity, a notion of pleasure, a notion of tranquility, a notion of a sentient being, a notion of a life-force, a notion of a soul, a notion of a mind-born being, a notion of a youth, and a notion of a self as an agent."
The arising of such various forms of non-knowing is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Within this sphere of ignorance, greed, hatred, and delusion arise; from that greed, hatred, and delusion, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) arise.
The designation for those objects is called "consciousness," and from that consciousness arise the four aggregates.
The sense faculties which serve as the basis for that name-and-form are the six sense bases.
The conjunction of these three factors is called "contact."
Contact gives rise to sensation;
through attachment to sensation, craving arises.
As craving expands, it is called grasping.
Grasping further gives rise to existence;
the karmic existence acts as the cause for the arising of the aggregates.
The maturation of these aggregates is called old age.
The disintegration of the aggregates is called death;
being deluded by craving, attached to it, and tormented by it is called sorrow;
the lamentation consisting of recollecting past events and uttering words of grief is called wailing.
That which is associated with the five bodies of consciousness is called suffering (*duḥkha*);
that which is a lack of mental gladness is called grief (*daurmanasya*);
and that which follows from secondary afflictions is called vexation (*upāyāsa*).
Ignorance is called "nescience" (avidyā);
volitional activity is called "formations" (saṃskāra);
and discernment is called "consciousness" (vijñāna).
Their mutual support is called name-and-form;
their dependence on a locus is called the six sense bases;
and their contact with objects is called contact.
Because it experiences and receives, it is called "feeling" (vedanā);
because it thirsts and craves, it is called "craving" (tṛṣṇā);
because it grasps and clings, it is called "clinging" (upādāna).
Grasping gives rise again to existence, and is therefore called "existence" (bhava);
it is able to produce [the aggregates], and is therefore called "birth" (jāti);
the faculties reach maturity, and is therefore called "old age" (jarā).
The disintegration and destruction [of the aggregates] is called death;
the sorrowful grief is called lamentation;
the state of dejection and frustration is called sighing.
Because the mind is not pleased, it is called sorrow (*daurmanasya*);
because it oppresses the body, it is called suffering (*duḥkha*);
because it does not accord with one's feelings, it is called vexation (*upāyāsa*).
Not practicing the practice of genuine cultivation is called wrong practice;
lack of knowledge is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because of the presence of ignorance, one performs various types of formative actions: meritorious formative actions, non-meritorious formative actions, and imperturbable formative actions.

When one performs actions that are meritorious near-approaches or non-meritorious near-approaches, this is called consciousness; therefore, it is said that "volitional formations have ignorance as their condition.

When one performs actions that are non-meritorious near-approaches or non-meritorious near-approaches, this too is consciousness; therefore, it is said that "consciousness has volitional formations as its condition."

The arising of the movement toward the immovable near-approach, and the one who moves toward the immovable near-approach, are also within consciousness; therefore, it is said that "consciousness conditions name-and-form.
As name-and-form increases, it acts as the gateway for the six sense bases; therefore, it is said that "name-and-form conditions the six sense bases."
The six sense bases evolve within the body; therefore, it is said that "with the six sense bases as condition, there is contact.
Contact of a similar kind gives rise to feeling of a similar kind; therefore, "with contact as condition, there is feeling.
One becomes attached to the distinctions of feeling with delight and joy; therefore, it is said that "with feeling as condition, there is craving."
Because one is attached to and relishes pleasure, craving does not let go; because one repeatedly seeks it with joy, it is called "craving conditions grasping.
Thus, through such seeking, there arises renewed existence (*bhava*), which gives rise to karma of body, speech, and mind; therefore, it is called "grasping conditions existence."
The arising of the five aggregates from karma is called "conditioned by existence, there is birth.
That which causes the aggregates born of birth to ripen, decay, and perish is called "conditioned by birth, there is aging and death.
These are what are known as the twelve links of dependent origination.

Acting as mutual causes for one another, they are neither permanent nor created, devoid of volition, and likewise without arising through conditions, without the nature of exhaustion, without the nature of detachment from desire, and without the nature of cessation; they have flowed and turned uninterruptedly since beginningless time, like the swift current of a river.

"Even if dependent origination proceeds without interruption like the swift current of a river, these twelve links of dependent origination function as the causal basis for the process through the conjunction of four factors."
What are the four? They are ignorance, craving, karma, and consciousness.

The self-nature of this consciousness-seed acts as the cause; the self-nature of the field of karma acts as the cause; and the self-nature of the afflictions of ignorance and craving act as the cause.
Karma, afflictions, and consciousness can produce seeds.
Thus, karma and consciousness act as the field for the seeds; craving and consciousness act as the moisture for the seeds; and ignorance and consciousness cause the seeds to sprout.
That karma does not form this thought:
"I am acting as a field for the seed of consciousness.
Craving does not form this thought:
"I provide moisture for the seed of consciousness.
Ignorance does not form this thought:
"I cause the seed of consciousness to sprout."
The seed of consciousness also does not form the thought:
"I am produced from various conditions.

Nevertheless, in reality, the seed of consciousness is established upon karma and afflictions; it is moistened by craving and covered with the soil of ignorance, thereby producing the sprout of name-and-form.

This sprout of name-and-form is not self-made, not made by another, not made by both together, not created by an omnipotent lord, not produced by the transformation of time, not born from primal nature (*svabhāva*), not dependent on a [single] cause, nor does it arise without a cause; nevertheless, it arises through the conjunction of the parents at the time of union, and through the continuity of the correspondence with other conditions.
This seed of consciousness gives rise to the sprout of name-and-form within the mother’s womb.

In the absence of a master and without a self as a recipient, when the conditions for phenomena—which are like illusory forms—are not lacking, visual consciousness arises from five kinds of conditions.
What are the five factors? They are:
the eye as the basis, visible forms as the object, light for illumination, space for non-obstruction, and the attention arising from these as the faculty of deliberation.

The visual consciousness relies upon the eye, takes visible forms as its objective support, uses light for illumination, and employs space for non-obstruction; the attention arising from these serves as the function of investigation.
If the various conditions are absent, visual consciousness does not arise.
If the internal sense base of the eye is lacking, as well as visible forms, light, space, and attention, then visual consciousness does not arise.
When these five conditions are not lacking, they all come together and are able to produce visual consciousness.
That eye does not form the thought:
"I act as the basis for visual consciousness."
That color does not form this thought:
"I serve as the object-condition for visual consciousness.
The light does not form this thought:
"I provide the condition of illumination for visual consciousness.
Space does not form this thought:
"I provide the condition of non-obstruction for visual consciousness."
The mental faculty that has arisen does not form this thought:
"I am performing deliberation for the visual consciousness.
Furthermore, the visual consciousness does not form this thought:
"I am produced by many conditions.
Indeed, visual consciousness arises from many conditions;
the other four sense faculties should be understood in the same way as before.
"In reality, there is no dharma that transmigrates from this world to another.
Yet, the designation of karmic retribution exists because its causes and conditions are not lacking.

It is like a bright mirror manifesting the image of a face; the face does not actually transfer into the mirror, yet the image of the face appears within the mirror because its causes and conditions are not lacking."
In this way, there is no passing away from here to another place;
yet, because the causes and conditions are not lacking, there is the manifestation of the fruition of karma.

It is like the lunar disk, which is forty thousand *yojanas* above the earth: when there is even a small amount of water in a vessel, the reflection of the moon appears therein. Yet, in reality, it does not perish there to appear within that small amount of water in the vessel; rather, through the conjunction of various conditions, the image manifests in such a manner.
It does not perish here to be born elsewhere; rather, there is a mutual resonance of karmic retribution because the causes and conditions are not lacking.
For example, if there is no fuel, fire will not arise;
if there is fuel, fire arises.
The seeds of consciousness produced by karma and afflictions continue from their place of origin, and the sprout of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) develops.

Thus, these phenomena—which are without a master, without a self, and without anything that possesses them—act as mutual causes and conditions; like illusory appearances, they are phenomena of intrinsic nature, with their causes and conditions remaining unimpaired.
"One should understand that internally conditioned phenomena have five characteristics:
they are neither eternal nor annihilated; they do not undergo transmigration; from a small cause a great fruit arises; and they arise as a continuous succession of similar [moments]."
How is it not eternal?
Because from the aggregates at this end one dies, and the aggregates at another end are born;
it is not that the very aggregates which die at this end are those same aggregates born at that end.
However, when the aggregates at the limit of death cease, the aggregates at the limit of birth arise; therefore, it is not eternal.
How is it not discontinuous?
It is because the aggregates at the limit of death do not first cease before the aggregates at the limit of birth arise.

Nor is it that the aggregates at the limit of death do not cease while, at that very moment, the aggregates of the intermediate state arise—like the rising and falling of a balance scale; this is called "non-interruption."
What is meant by "not transferring"?
It is called "not transferring" because it occurs prior to the transition into a different category.
What is meant by "the cause being small while the fruit is great"?
If one performs a small amount of wholesome or unwholesome karma in this body, one will receive a great deal of wholesome or unwholesome retribution in a future body.
How is there a continuity of similarity?
It is just as when one performs an action in the body currently being experienced, one receives the retribution for it immediately in the next life.

If one practices for a long time with the eye of right wisdom according to reality regarding these dependently arisen phenomena—seeing them as being without a person, without a self, non-erroneous, unarisen, unceasing, uncreated, unconditioned, unobstructed, without an object of perception, quiescent, fearless, indestructible, inexhaustible, like an illusion, empty and still by nature, insubstantial, like a wound, like an abscess, resistant, impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self—then one does not circulate in the past, wondering: "Did I exist in the past?"
"Who was I in the past? How did I exist in the past?
Furthermore, they flow toward the future, thinking:
"Will I exist in the future? Who is it that says 'I will exist in the future'? How will I exist in the future?"
"Will I not exist in the future?
Who says that I will not exist in the future? How will I not exist in the future?"
Furthermore, one does not transmigrate into the middle period, thinking: "Do I exist now?
Who says that I exist now?"
"What is meant by 'I exist now'?
Where will this sentient being go after passing away from here?

All those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world who hold divergent views—namely, those bound by the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-span, various views, and the bonds of hope and auspiciousness—if they are endowed with right view, at this time they sever all fetters and realize universal knowledge (*parijñā*).

Like a *tāla* tree that has been cut down, being of a nature of non-existence, they enter into the ultimate truth; throughout the long duration of all realms of existence, they realize non-arising and non-ceasing, attain the perfection of patience (*kṣānti*), and extensively perform boundless deeds for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, for even a brief moment, carefully and profoundly contemplate the principles of dependent origination within this sutra, they shall be able to instantly extinguish the most grave karmic obstructions accumulated since beginningless time; they will extensively gather merit and virtue, attain penetrating wisdom, forever sever false views, and preach the Dharma with fearlessness.
"Venerable Śāriputra!
The Bhagavān has bestowed upon those sons and daughters of good family the prophecy of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

When the Venerable Śāriputra, along with the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, heard this sūtra spoken by the Bodhisattva Maitreya, their hearts were filled with great joy; they gave rise to profound sympathetic rejoicing, rose from their seats, prostrated at the feet of the Bodhisattva Maitreya, and joyfully put it into practice.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Simile of the Rice Seedling Explaining Dependent Origination, Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
